t: A republic is a state without a monarch, governed as the “public thing”, res publica, by officials elected for limited terms who answer to the law and to the citizens.
From Rome to Venice, Florence and the Dutch Republic, most early republics were run by a narrow elite of patricians, nobles or merchants rather than by all their citizens.
Since the American and French revolutions the republic has become the usual form of the state: in 2017, 159 of the world’s 206 sovereign states had “republic” in their official names.
dyk: San Marino, by tradition founded in 301, calls itself the world’s oldest surviving republic; its heads of state, two Captains Regent who rule jointly, still serve for only six months at a time.
ev: By Roman tradition the last king, Tarquinius Superbus, is expelled and the first two consuls are elected
The lex Hortensia gives the decisions of the plebeian assembly the force of law for all Romans
Octavian takes the name Augustus; the republic’s forms survive under the rule of one man
The Serrata restricts Venice’s Great Council to the families already sitting in it
The States General take sovereignty for themselves, founding the Dutch Republic
The Declaration of Independence rejects the British monarchy; the American states adopt republican constitutions
The National Convention abolishes the French monarchy and proclaims the First Republic
The German and Austrian monarchies fall and both countries are proclaimed republics

f.power: Elected magistrates, councils and assemblies who hold office for limited terms under the law; there is no hereditary monarch
f.legitimacy: The state as res publica, the “public thing” of its citizens governed under law, not the property of a ruling family
f.chosen: Officials are elected for fixed terms, often in colleges of two or more; in older republics only a narrow body of patricians, nobles or merchants could vote or stand
f.examples: the Roman Republic (509–27 BCE), the Republic of Venice (697–1797), the Republic of Florence (1115–1532), the Dutch Republic (1588–1795), the United States (since 1776), the French Third Republic (1870–1940)
